brief.title: Return Deadline Assistant
brief.customer: Frequent US online shoppers who sometimes return electronics or marketplace purchases at large retailers.
brief.problem: Shoppers who already want to return an item can lose track of the deadline or follow the wrong rule when an order involves a marketplace seller, delayed delivery, or a membership exception.
brief.solution: Use a redacted receipt or selected order details to show a return deadline card, the retailer rule supporting it, any facts still needed, and an optional reminder.
brief.known: Public return policies are available for some retailers. The team has not measured whether shoppers use sourced guidance or pay for it.

assumptions.statement: Receipt forwarding and automatic deadline reminders give the product a distinct reason to switch.
assumptions.reason: A generic reminder needs to beat alternatives on more than convenience if the same intake and reminder workflow is already on offer.

assumptions.statement: Shoppers facing a policy exception will use source-linked guidance instead of a generic deadline reminder.
assumptions.reason: Source-linked guidance could matter when choosing which deadline to act on. Product descriptions and policy pages provide no usage evidence for this audience.

assumptions.statement: The retailer name and order date are enough to determine a reliable return deadline.
assumptions.reason: A reminder can mislead when a different date starts the clock or a seller follows a separate rule.

assumptions.statement: Frequent shoppers will pay a recurring fee after using the service for two attempted returns.
assumptions.reason: The opportunity is episodic. A repeat-use or pricing test needs to precede any revenue estimate.

assumptions.statement: A first version can show buyers checkable return rules from official pages for two initial retailers.
assumptions.reason: A narrow launch needs public policy text it can link and explain. A confirmed deadline still depends on what is known about the order.

sources.title: Return Window · Getting started
sources.passage: Our system automatically detects the retailer, extracts your order details, and calculates when your return window closes based on the store's policy.

sources.title: Roundtrip Returns · Developer's App Store description
sources.passage: Email forwarding (optional) — forward an order email to your private address, and the return shows up parsed and ready

sources.title: Best Buy · Return and exchange periods
sources.passage: the time period begins the day you receive your product

sources.title: Target · Returns and exceptions
sources.passage: Some items sold by Target have a modified return policy noted on the receipt, packing slip

links.reason: Return Window advertises order-detail extraction and policy-based deadline calculation from forwarded emails.
Roundtrip also advertises order-email forwarding followed by automatic parsing.
Retailer policy exceptions make a verification interaction worth testing. The policy offers no evidence that shoppers will choose that interaction.
The clock can start on receipt rather than purchase. An order date alone can produce the wrong deadline.
Item-level policy can differ from the store's default. The system needs a way to identify or flag these cases.
The retailer publishes a rule the tool can display for a relevant Best Buy scenario.
Target publishes where to check for item-level exceptions. This supports a narrow, source-linked walkthrough.

experiment.title: Compare a sourced deadline card with a standard reminder
experiment.procedure: Recruit 12 frequent online shoppers. Use fictional orders so nobody shares private receipts. Give each shopper two matched exception cases and rotate which case uses a plain reminder or a card with a policy source and missing-fact prompt. Ask them to act on each order and then choose a format for a third order. Score their choices against a checklist written before testing.
experiment.metric: Number of participants who handle the exception correctly with the sourced card and choose that format for a third order.
experiment.threshold: Move to a two-retailer pilot if at least 8 of 12 qualify. Below 8, review where people misunderstood the policy or preferred the simpler reminder.
experiment.time: One week for recruiting and 15-minute sessions
experiment.cost: $0 in software for a clickable mockup, excluding research labor and any participant incentives
